transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Could you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, thank you. I suppose what finally got me to actually make an appointment is that my concentration has just gotten completely unreliable lately. 

I’ll be at the clinic—I’m a dentist, you see, have been for nearly forty years. The field has changed so much, honestly. The composite resins we use now are completely different from when I started in the eighties. We’ve been having the absolute worst time with our supply chain lately, trying to get the right bonding agents. My supplier, Dave, he says it's a shipping delay at the ports, but I don't know... anyway, I'm sorry, what was I saying? 

Right, my focus. I'll be reviewing a patient's chart at the office, or even at home trying to lay out a watercolor wash—I do watercolors on the weekends, mostly coastal scenes. You have to use a really good heavy, cold-pressed paper or the water just pools and ruins the gradient, it's a whole delicate process. But I’ll be sitting there, and suddenly I realize I’ve read the exact same line in the dental chart three times, or my brush is just hovering there drying out. My mind just completely wanders off to... well, to everything that could possibly go wrong.
Have you been feeling down, sad, or losing interest in activities that you usually enjoy, like your watercolor painting or anything else?

No, no, I wouldn't say I've been feeling down or sad. I still look forward to painting, really I do. I just bought this new set of Kolinsky sable brushes. Oh, they are magnificent. They hold water like you wouldn't believe, which is essential for getting those really seamless skies. My wife, Susan, she always says I spend too much on art supplies, but you know, you get what you pay for. It’s like with dental instruments—if you buy cheap explorers, the tips bend, and then how are you supposed to detect a micro-cavity? You just can't. You need that tactile feedback. 

But anyway, no, I haven't lost interest. I still want to do things. It's just that when I sit down to do them, I can't seem to stay present. I'm just... elsewhere. But not sad, no.
Do you ever find yourself having thoughts that you don’t want, that seem intrusive or bothersome, and that you can’t seem to get rid of no matter how hard you try?

Intrusive thoughts? Well... I wouldn't say I have thoughts that I can't get rid of, like an obsession or anything. It's not like a song stuck in my head. Have you ever had that happen, by the way? Where you hear one line of a song at the grocery store—they always play the strangest mix at the Stop & Shop down the street. Last week I went in just to get some lemons. Susan is very particular about having fresh lemons for her tea, she drinks this Earl Grey that she orders special from London. The bergamot oil in it is very strong, almost medicinal, but she swears by it. 

Anyway, they were playing some old disco song, and I couldn't get the bassline out of my head for three days. It was driving me absolutely up the wall while I was trying to do a root canal. A root canal requires absolute precision, you know. If you miss a supplementary canal, the whole tooth can get reinfected, and then the patient is back in your chair in six months in agony. It's a terrible situation. 

But no, I don't have thoughts like that, not bothersome ones that I'm trying to force away. It's more just the worrying, like I mentioned before. My mind just drifts off into worrying about things, but I wouldn't call them unwanted intrusive thoughts.
Do you find yourself worrying about things much more than usual, even when there isn't a clear reason, and does it feel like you can't stop worrying even when you try?

Well, yes, actually. That's exactly it. My mind just keeps circling around all sorts of things constantly. I'm in the middle of transitioning out of my practice, you see, getting ready to retire. The young fellow taking over, Dr. Peterson, he's very bright, went to Tufts—excellent dental program there, really top-notch clinical exposure. But he has this habit of rushing through the initial exams. I always spent at least twenty minutes just talking to the patient before I even picked up a mirror. You build trust that way. I remember Mrs. Gable, she was terrified of dentists, absolutely petrified because of a bad extraction in the seventies. It took me three appointments just to get her comfortable enough for a cleaning. 

But I sit there and I just worry incessantly about whether my old patients are going to be looked after properly. And then it spirals into whether the financial side of the practice handoff is sound, because the valuation was done right when interest rates spiked. We had to renegotiate the seller financing three times. My accountant, Larry, he's been doing my books since 1992, he says it's fine, but I can't stop thinking about it. 

And then... well, I worry about what on earth I'm going to do with myself when I'm fully retired. Am I just going to become completely useless? Susan says we'll travel, maybe go to Tuscany. Have you been? The light there for painting is supposed to be incredible. The Renaissance painters, they understood light in a way that just baffles the modern mind. But even when I think about Tuscany, I start worrying about our passports expiring, or getting sick overseas. It just never stops. It feels completely out of proportion, even to me, but I just can't seem to turn it off no matter what I do.

latest_inference.note: The patient reports persistent and excessive worry about multiple aspects of life (e.g., work, health, retirement, future plans), difficulty controlling the worry, and impaired concentration, which aligns with generalized anxiety disorder (F48.1). Other candidates (F06.81, F06.82, F06.89) are ruled out due to absence of symptoms specific to those disorders such as mood disturbances, obsessive-compulsive features, or other psychotic or organic symptoms.

No significant exclusions yet due to the early stage of the interview.
